measured-scalar.description: The latest scalar emitted by a repeatable measurement source. Authored lf-num text freezes the value a version states; the source snapshot records whether that measurement ran again.

text-document.description: UTF-8 text captured from a file or a selected line range.

lf-ask.description: One complete Ask for the reader: begin with one direct heading stating the question, then include any context or evidence needed to answer it and exactly one non-quoted widget whose entry declares a local Ask through x-awaits or x-request.ask. The nested widget still owns the action or external-request lifecycle and determines whether the Ask is open. The authored heading is the Ask's title: it stays in the document's reading, gives the Asks tray its name, and is where `a`/`A` arrives. Keep an ordinary semantic section around the Ask when the document needs a section landmark. The wrapper adds no frame or caption of its own.
lf-ask.x-example:
What should a full store do?

The beta never reached the cap. This decides what the first workspace at it sees.

Drop the oldest documents Editing continues. My take: this keeps work moving without losing server data. Pause offline editing Nothing leaves.

lf-gloss.description: A short, plain-text explanation attached to a phrase: hover the phrase to glance at it, Tab to its Explain control to reach it by keyboard, or click or tap the phrase to keep it open; Escape and a click elsewhere close it. Use one for a local term, acronym, or premise whose meaning a reader may want without leaving the sentence — not for a citation, a qualification the argument depends on, or an aside long enough to deserve visible prose, a details disclosure, or a sidenote. The phrase and `tip` are both the page's words: the phrase stays in its sentence, and the explanation can be selected, quoted, and commented on while open. A static copy or printout puts the explanation after the phrase as a quiet parenthetical note, so no authored meaning depends on hover or script; keep the phrase out of parentheses of your own, or that copy nests them. Keep the explanation self-contained and write it at the first useful occurrence rather than marking every repetition.
lf-gloss.x-example: Deploy through a <lf-gloss tip="A thin, end-to-end path through the real system.">walking skeleton</lf-gloss> before parallelizing.

lf-num.description: One measured scalar frozen into the sentence that states it. Write the displayed value, unit included, as the element text; bind `source` to the repeatable measurement feed and set `at` to that source snapshot's recorded `updated` instant. A later `leaf data set` on the same source makes `version check` advise that this number is stale without replacing what an older version says. `via` may preserve the human-readable command or query in markup when the source id alone is not enough provenance. Use lf-metric instead when the number is a headline KPI in a metric row, and ordinary text for a number that is not produced by a repeatable measurement.
lf-num.x-example: The import now takes <lf-num source="import-latency" at="2026-08-27T09:00:00Z" via="uv run bench-import">184 ms</lf-num> at p95.

lf-source.description: A file-backed text document supplied through Leaf data. `source` binds the page-owned feed. `snapshot` selects an immutable capture; omit it to follow the current value. `language` colors the source with one of $languages. The capture's label and selected line range appear above the exact text. Put the widget inside ordinary details or an lf-tab when the source should begin collapsed or in a separate view.

lf-toc.description: A table of contents derived from the page's h2-h6 headings. `max-level` sets the deepest heading included when lower-level headings are local detail rather than page destinations; omitting it includes every level. A page with two or more included headings places one in an `aside.sidebar` near the opening by default; omit it when the page is compact enough that its outline is already visible at a glance. In the roomy margin, the runtime distributes the page title and headings down a full-height spine according to the sections they lead, paints the visible band of the document on that spine, and reveals the generated labels on pointer or keyboard entry. If the expanded labels would crowd, only the destination under the pointer or keyboard focus reveals. In flow, on paper, and in a standalone copy, it remains an ordinary open outline. Existing heading ids become link targets. For an id-less heading, the widget adds a position-derived target beside it without changing the authored heading. Live links reveal headings inside disclosures or tabs, and a copied link returns to the same version's section. A stable authored heading id keeps that target across versions. The generated labels are link apparatus rather than a second commentable copy of each heading, and version diffs ignore them as generated navigation. Write the element empty and give it a stable id.
lf-toc.x-example:
Migration plan

Prepare

Take a snapshot.

Check capacity

Leave headroom for the copy.

Move

Shift one cohort at a time.

lf-options.description: The alternatives in a question the reader answers. Put a live group inside lf-ask, where one ordinary heading states the question and any premise or evidence shared by every alternative can lead into the choices; the group itself contains only options and controls. Children are lf-option elements only. An option leading with a <strong> title becomes a full-width card; put its case and decision-relevant evidence or preview there instead of in separate alternative sections. Bare-label options render as compact rows for alternatives that need no case beyond the label. A row may use `for` only when the choice selects among sections or work items that already exist independently of the decision; do not create sections merely to hold the alternatives. With `choose` (which requires an id), the group draws as one control and takes the reader's pick by click or keyboard. `multiple` (which requires `choose`) allows a set. The marks say "choose one" or "choose any" to a screen reader; do not repeat that instruction in the question. On the page the last cell is an `Another option` field for an answer the author did not list. Tab reaches the field, Enter writes a newline, and Mod+Enter adds the option. Adding creates and selects a real option through the same `choose` action, whose optional `additions` maps every generated option id to its words; it does not start a thread. In a thread the thread's reply box already owns that role, Enter from an option mark continues there, and a multiple group adds a Done press whose `answer` action states the set is complete. The pick reaches the agent as a `choose` action naming every picked option. Generated options remain effective across revisions and can receive a separate clarification thread. An author may incorporate one as an ordinary lf-option with the same id and words. Authored `chosen` can record the pick, but replay already preserves it; rewriting a picked option needs `restated`. `settled` (also requiring an id) collapses a retired decision to a disclosure naming the chosen option while preserving every option and anchor. A live choose group remains an open Ask until a pick rests on it or its thread's declared completion arrives.
lf-options.x-example:
Where should run status appear?

Both choices preserve the existing run detail.

effort: lowrisk: medrecommended Status on the run list One join; failures are visible without a click. effort: nonerisk: low Leave the list alone No work; failures stay one click away.

lf-option.description: One alternative in a decision. Default to a <strong> title and one sentence naming the consequence. When comparison facts help, show the same two or three chips across its siblings. Keep decision-relevant evidence or a preview inside the option, but add a fact rail, paragraphs, or a nested visual only when the choice cannot be made from that compact face. A short label alone renders as a compact row for an alternative that needs no case beyond the label. `for` may point that row at an existing section or work item only when the target remains useful independently of this decision; it never supplies the row's words. `chosen` records the reader's pick in authored state. An ordinary chip such as `<lf-chip tone="ok">recommended</lf-chip>` may mark the author's preferred option; write it after the comparison chips and keep the reason as ordinary prose in that option. Rewriting a picked option needs `restated`; the other options may change freely.

lf-chip.description: One short label in the band above an option's or a variant's title. Comparison chips name what the alternatives differ on, in the words that fit them. `effort: low` and `risk: high` are worth starting from, since most decisions do turn on those two, but they are a suggestion and nothing more — `blast-radius: high`, `backward compat: no`, `cost: £240`, `migration: two tables` are the same slot, and a chip is as free in its answer as in its name: a scale of your own, a yes or a no, a quantity, a few words. Write comparison chips before the <strong> title (a lf-variant takes them the same way, being the same shape without the decision), and write the same ones on every option in the group, in the same order, so they read down it. An ordinary final chip such as `<lf-chip tone="ok">recommended</lf-chip>` may mark the author's preferred option, while the reason stays in the option's prose. It is advice, while `chosen` alone records the reader's pick. Chips are the glance and not the comparison — two or three an eye takes in before it reads, where a `<dl class="facts">` rail is the dimensions the options are argued on at whatever length that takes. An option can carry both, and only the rail costs a card its terseness: a `<dl>` is block content, so it stacks the group into rows, and chips never do. `tone` tints a chip — the layer's own vocabulary, `$tones.names`, which the author can query in `registry.json` — and is the author's judgement about this answer, not a property of the facet: `risk: high` is red because you say so, and the same word on another page may not be. Leave it off and the chip is neutral, which is what most of them should be; colour that lands on every chip has stopped pointing at anything. It is the same bargain `lf-metric` makes with `direction` — the theme knows the tints, the author knows which way is good.

lf-milestones.description: A timeline of milestones with status dots on a rail. Children are lf-milestone elements only.
lf-milestones.x-example: Survey the sites Map sun and squirrel routes. Build the feeders Two classic, two heated. Install and watch

lf-milestone.description: One milestone. Lead with a <strong> title; prose follows. `status` colors the timeline dot; `when` is a free-text schedule label; `tags` is a comma-separated list rendered as chips.

lf-timeline.description: A chronological event log — the incident-report shape. Children are lf-event elements only. Where lf-milestones tracks planned work by status, lf-timeline records what happened, when.
lf-timeline.x-example: Feeder camera offline Battery alert from the north feeder. Battery swapped Camera back Feed resumed.

lf-event.description: One event on a timeline. Lead with a <strong> title; prose follows. `at` is a free-text time label; `kind` colors the dot.

lf-compare.description: Labeled variants — neutral exhibition, where lf-options is a decision. Children are lf-variant elements only. Layout follows lf-options: terse variants sit side by side, block content in any variant stacks the group into rows, and a `<dl class="facts">` after the label docks as an aligned rail.
lf-compare.x-example: Cedar Weathers silver; no sealant. Pine Cheaper; seal it yearly.

lf-variant.description: One variant in a comparison. Lead with a <strong> label; any content follows, widgets included.

lf-metrics.description: A KPI row. Children are lf-metric elements only.
lf-metrics.x-example:
<lf-metrics>
  <lf-metric id="k-visits" value="312" delta="+41" direction="up-good">daily visits</lf-metric>
  <lf-metric id="k-refills" value="2.1/wk" delta="+0.4" direction="up-bad">refills</lf-metric>
  <lf-metric id="k-species" value="14">species seen</lf-metric>
</lf-metrics>

lf-metric.description: One metric: element text is the label, `value` the headline number, `delta` a signed change (leading + or -), `direction` says which sign is good (up-good, up-bad) so the delta colors honestly; without it the delta stays neutral.

lf-tree.description: A file tree from an indent-notation body: one node per line, children indented deeper, a trailing / marking a directory, trailing +N/-N tokens rendering as change badges. Body is data — text inside its <pre>, HTML-escaped (& first, then < and >).
lf-tree.x-example:
feeders/
  mount.py  +2 -2
  schedule.py  +1
  sites/
    north.toml

lf-code.description: An annotated code block — the walkthrough shape. The body is the code verbatim inside its <pre> (data, HTML-escaped — & first, then < and > — column 0); `language` colors it, naming one of $languages; `hi` highlights line ranges ("3-5,8"); lf-note children sit beside that <pre> and anchor remarks at lines by number. Leave `language` off where the body isn't source (a transcript, command output) — nothing guesses, so an undeclared block stays plain.
lf-code.x-example:
def bracket(temp):
    if temp < 0:
        return "steel"
    return "cedar"
Freezing is the only threshold that matters.

lf-note.description: A remark anchored at a line of its lf-code parent. Prose content; `at` is the 1-based line number.

lf-chart.description: A chart drawn from a comma-separated body: the header row names the x column and then one column per series, and every row after it is one x value and its numbers (blank where a series has none). The body is data, not prose: text inside its <pre>, HTML-escaped (& first, then the angle brackets). `kind` says which picture — bars (a group of bars per x value), rows (horizontal bars, for long names or a ranking), stack (bars stacked into a total, so no negatives), line (a run over time or an ordered x), dots (two numbers against each other, x column numeric). `y` names what the numbers are. A bar's x is one slot per row whatever it says; a line or a scatter reads its column, so dates (2026-06-01, or 2026-06 for a month) get a time axis and numbers a numeric one. Two rows may not share an x value, and a series column may not be empty. At most $series.steps series — fold the small ones together or split the chart. There is no pie, because the comparison it asks for is between angles and the comparison bars ask for is between lengths. Comments anchor to the required id, not to text inside the drawing.
lf-chart.x-example:
week, backend, frontend
2026-05-04, 31, 18
2026-05-11, 26, 21
2026-05-18, 19, 14
2026-05-25, 12, 11

lf-shot.description: A before/after pair of screenshots in one fixed frame. Click the target’s round Button or the image to flip between states. A rail above the image keeps Before at the left and After at the right; a short accent rule marks the visible state. The Button’s split circle fills the left half for before and the right half for after, and its hover label names the next view. Image clicks and Space keep working in standalone exports. `before` and `after` are served image paths — `leaf page media <page> <file>…` copies author-chosen files into the page directory and prints the path to write; a screenshot is far too many bytes to inline. `alt` says what the pair shows, for a reader who can't see it. The element takes no content: what the page has to say about the change is ordinary prose written around it, where the user can quote it. Where the change is what a decision turns on, the pair goes inside the lf-option proposing it, so the reader flips it and presses in one place. Reach for it when the change reads at page scale — layout, spacing, a component swapped out. Below that scale the column's width is against you: crop the pair to the part that moved, or show the element itself before and after at real size.
lf-shot.x-example:
The option cards

The chips now sit above the title, so a scanning eye reads cost before prose.

lf-board.description: A kanban board the user edits directly: cards move between columns or reorder within one — dragged by the grip, or by keyboard (the grip is a button: Enter grabs, arrows move, Enter drops) — and each completed move reaches the agent as a `move` action naming the card, target column, and position. Children are lf-column elements only. Write the board as you mean it and leave it alone afterwards: a recorded move carries onto every later version by itself, so re-emitting a card where you first put it does not undo the user's move. Replay preserves the exact position, but the reader-origin mark, version diff, and restatement gate compare a card's column only: a reorder within one column is deliberately not called out as a separate state change, because raw indexes do not compose when neighbouring cards move. A move rests on its card, so revising one they have moved is the card's `restated` (see `$restated` in `registry.json`), never the board's.
lf-board.x-example: Heated perch Wire the south feeder. Squirrel baffle Camera mount

lf-column.description: One column on a board. `label` is the column heading, and the name a screen reader announces for the list of cards beneath it — so it has to read as the column's name on its own. Children are lf-card elements only; an empty column is a valid drop target.

lf-card.description: One card on a board. Lead with a <strong> title; prose follows. The user drags it by its grip; the id names it in `move` actions and keeps comment anchors stable across moves. Rewriting a card the user has moved needs `restated` on the card (see `$restated` in `registry.json`), which retracts the moves of that card alone — the rest of the board keeps its arrangement.

lf-tabs.description: Workstreams on one page: use one family when several are live at once. Keep the shared title and lede before it, put the current stream first, and remove an earlier run once the current work no longer depends on it, keeping the context it still needs, and any passage whose id anchors an open thread or holds a standing decision, in a collapsed details inside the relevant tab. Ordering gives the first panel emphasis and makes it the default for a reader with no remembered panel or reading position. A saved panel or restored position takes precedence because the open tab is the reader's view state — remembered per browser tab like scroll position, never an action, never carried by a version. Each lf-tab is a self-contained sub-context with its own prose and widgets, while Threads, Asks, versions, and sign-off remain global. Find-in-page, Ask travel, and comment-anchor jumps open the owning tab. Children are lf-tab elements only; unupgraded, panels stack as labeled sections.
lf-tabs.x-example:
Wire the first site this week.

Keep the original outcome and constraints in reach.

lf-tab.description: One workstream panel. `label` names its tab in the strip (and the stacked heading before upgrade); content is open — prose, sections, and other widgets nest freely. Ids inside share the page's one universe, so keep them distinct across tabs.

lf-draft.description: A block of text the user owns: they press it (or its ✎ button) to rewrite it in place, and the exact words reach the agent as an `edit` action naming the element. After the first edit, Changes shows a bounded, lossless word-aligned difference from this version, every recorded body in order, and a Restore control for each older body; very large divergent middles appear as one replacement rather than freezing the page. Restoring posts another ordinary `edit`, so it converges across tabs and later versions instead of creating private undo state. The body is the draft text verbatim inside its <pre> (data, HTML-escaped — & first, then < and >; newlines preserved). It carries no Ask chrome of its own — put a draft inside a lf-card where the column is the verdict, or let page sign-off approve the page as a whole. Usable anywhere prose flows. The agent rewriting prose of its own goes in a lf-suggestion instead; a draft is the user's own words, so there is nothing for them to accept. Once they have edited one those words are theirs: re-emit the body you wrote and their edit still stands over it — and `leaf comment` reads it their way, quoting the words their edit left and refusing the ones it replaced. To take the pen back — a fact of yours to fix in a sentence they rewrote — write the new text and mark the element `restated` (see `$restated` in `registry.json`).
lf-draft.x-example: Adds --dry-run to every mutating command.

lf-specimen.description: Quoted material: a region the page exhibits rather than speaks — a sample decision, a demo board, markup shown as an example. Renders as quotation: a muted left gutter beside the quoted region, with a small-caps "quoted" line above it (`label` extends that line — "quoted · a decision"). Content is open and renders at full fidelity, but it is a mention, not a use: interactive widgets inside are inert — a choose group takes no clicks, a board no drags, a suggestion no decision. Keep the content visibly fictional, and let the gutter do the marking: a caption explaining that the region is an example is the page narrating a widget it could just use.
lf-specimen.x-example: effort: lowPaper maps Nothing to charge. effort: medDedicated GPS Offline maps, week-long battery. My take: this is the better field tool.

ok.means: good — keep this; no change asked

cut.means: too long — shorten or remove this

more.means: needs support — expand or substantiate this
